difficultyRationale: A practical design-choice question rather than a trivia question: it checks whether the candidate can map a real requirement (nested, validated, testable config) to the tool built for it.
prompt: A team needs to bind a block of related configuration — `app.mail.host`, `app.mail.port`, `app.mail.retries` — into a single Java object, validate that `port` is within 1-65535, and unit-test that binding without starting a full Spring context. Which approach fits best, and why?
explanation: `@ConfigurationProperties` is designed exactly for this: it binds a whole related block of properties onto one type-safe class in a single step, supports JSR-303/`@Validated` constraints on its fields, and the resulting POJO can be constructed and validated in a plain unit test by binding a `Map` or `Properties` source, with no Spring context required. `@Value` injects one property expression at a time into one field and has no comparable support for nested structures or constraint validation.

options.text: `@ConfigurationProperties`, because it binds a whole nested structure onto a type-safe class in one step, works with `@Validated`/JSR-303 constraints on the fields, and the class can be tested by binding a `Map`/`Properties` source without a full Spring context.
options.explanation: Correct — this is precisely the use case `@ConfigurationProperties` targets, as distinct from `@Value`'s one-property-at-a-time injection.

options.text: `@Value`, because it is a single annotation and is therefore always the simplest choice, regardless of how many related properties are involved or whether the values need any structure or validation applied to them.
options.explanation: `@Value` injects one expression into one field; binding three related properties into a validated, nested object with it means hand-wiring three separate `@Value` fields and writing validation logic yourself — simpler in appearance, not in practice, for this case.

options.text: `@ConfigurationProperties` and `@Value` are interchangeable here; the choice between them is purely stylistic, since both ultimately resolve property keys against the same `Environment` and `PropertySource` chain underneath, with no real difference in capability.
options.explanation: They are not interchangeable for this requirement: only `@ConfigurationProperties` supports binding a nested block as one object with validation, which `@Value` does not provide at all.

options.text: Neither is appropriate; configuration like this has to be read manually from `Environment` at startup, by calling `getProperty()` for each key and wiring the validation logic by hand in a `@PostConstruct` method.
options.explanation: Manual `Environment` lookups are exactly what `@ConfigurationProperties` is meant to replace — it is the supported, documented mechanism for structured configuration binding.
